**Vignette: Marisol**

Marisol is a 38-year-old Guatemalan woman who has lived in the United States for eleven years. She works the early shift at a food processing plant, arriving before dawn and standing at the same station on the line for eight or nine hours, sorting and packaging. She is known among her coworkers as dependable, quiet, and quick with her hands. She rarely misses a shift. Until recently, work was the one place where the noise of the machinery and the rhythm of the conveyor belt made it possible to stop thinking.

Fourteen months ago, Marisol's younger brother, Tomás, was killed in a car accident two blocks from her apartment. He had come to visit her for the weekend — his first trip to see her in three years — and on the evening of his second day, he walked to the corner store to buy something she had forgotten. A driver ran a red light. Marisol did not witness the collision, but she heard the impact from her kitchen window. She went outside before she understood what had happened. She found him in the street before the ambulance arrived. She held his hand while he was still warm. He was twenty-six years old.

In the weeks that followed, Marisol moved through her days as though she were watching herself from a distance. She returned to the factory because she did not know what else to do, and because she needed the money. But something had shifted in the architecture of ordinary life. The walk from the bus stop to the plant takes her past an intersection with a traffic light, and every morning when the light turns red, her chest seizes. She has begun taking a longer route that adds fifteen minutes to her commute, though she has told no one why.

At the line, she sometimes loses stretches of time. A coworker will say something to her and she will realize she has not heard a word, that she has been somewhere else entirely — back in the street, in the dark, with Tomás's hand going cool in hers. The packages pile up wrong and the supervisor has spoken to her twice. She apologizes and rights herself, but the shame of it sits on top of everything else.

Sleep is where she is least safe. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with her heart hammering, her nightgown damp, the details of the dream already dissolving but the feeling of it — the helplessness, the specific quality of that silence — still entirely present. She lies in the dark of her one-bedroom apartment and does not try to go back to sleep. She watches the ceiling and waits for the alarm.

She has stopped calling her mother in Guatemala as often as she used to. Her mother wants to talk about Tomás, to remember him, and Marisol cannot do this yet. When his name comes up, something closes in her. She has told her mother she is very busy. This is partly true and partly a lie she tells herself as well.

She does not go out much. A few women from the plant have invited her to things — a birthday dinner, a quinceañera — and she has declined each time, offering the excuse of fatigue, which is genuine but not the whole story. The whole story is that she does not trust herself in public, does not trust that she will not suddenly be somewhere else, back in that street, in a way that others will notice and she will not be able to explain.

What she carries most heavily is not grief in the way she expected grief to feel. It is the image of his face when she reached him, and the particular thought that has attached itself to that image and will not let go: that she sent him out. She had forgotten the milk. She is the one who forgot the milk.
